intro: No treatment for POIS has been tested in a randomised controlled trial. Everything below comes from case reports, small studies or personal accounts, and what helps one person may not help another. This is general information, not advice: talk to a clinician before starting, stopping or combining anything.

anecdotal.label: Personal accounts
anecdotal.description: Experiences shared by individuals, for example on forums. Not published or checked studies.

caseReports.label: Case reports
caseReports.description: Published descriptions of one or a few individual patients. The weakest form of published evidence: there is no comparison group.

smallStudies.label: Small studies
smallStudies.description: Published results from a small group of patients, usually without a comparison group, so improvement can't be separated from chance or placebo.

entries.title: Antihistamines
entries.summary: Antihistamines block histamine, a chemical the body releases during allergic reactions. Because POIS often includes allergy-like symptoms such as a blocked nose and itchy eyes, some doctors have tried them.
reported: A published case report described a patient whose symptoms improved substantially on a daily antihistamine.
They are among the most commonly tried options in patient communities, with mixed results.
cautions: Some cause drowsiness: take care with driving or machinery.
Ask a pharmacist about interactions with other medicines.

sources.label: POIS successfully managed with antihistamine: a case report (PMC)
Post orgasmic illness syndrome: what do we know till now? (review, PMC)

entries.title: Alpha-blockers
entries.summary: Alpha-blockers relax smooth muscle and are usually prescribed for prostate or blood-pressure problems. They have been tried in POIS on the idea that the nervous-system response around ejaculation may play a part.
reported: Small reports and patient surveys describe some people getting partial relief.
sideEffects: Dizziness or light-headedness, especially when standing up
Reduced or absent ejaculation with some of these medicines
cautions: Can lower blood pressure: take care if you already take blood-pressure medicines.

sources.label: Post orgasmic illness syndrome: what do we know till now? (review, PMC)

entries.title: NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory painkillers)
entries.summary: NSAIDs reduce inflammation, and POIS has been linked to an inflammatory or immune response. Some patients take them around the time of an episode.
reported: Individual case reports and patient accounts describe some improvement in flu-like symptoms.
sideEffects: Stomach upset, and with regular use stomach ulcers or bleeding
cautions: Not suitable for everyone, for example people with stomach ulcers, kidney problems, some heart conditions or asthma triggered by NSAIDs.
Ask a doctor before regular or long-term use.

sources.label: Post orgasmic illness syndrome: what do we know till now? (review, PMC)

entries.title: Hyposensitization (autologous semen injections)
entries.summary: Based on the idea that POIS may be an allergic reaction to one's own semen, this treatment gives gradually increasing doses of the person's diluted semen under the skin over a long period, similar to allergy desensitisation.
reported: Small studies from the Netherlands reported improvement in many participants over courses lasting months to years.
sideEffects: Reactions where the injection is given
A possible risk of more serious allergic reactions
cautions: Only under a specialist, usually an allergist or immunologist, with a proper protocol.

sources.label: Intensified hyposensitization is an effective treatment of POIS (PMC)

entries.title: Hormonal treatments
entries.summary: Some people with POIS turn out to have low hormone levels, such as low testosterone. In those cases, doctors have tried treating the hormone problem.
reported: Case reports describe symptoms resolving in men with low testosterone who were treated by a specialist.
sideEffects: Depends on the hormone: can affect fertility, red blood cell levels, mood, skin and more
cautions: Only with blood tests and monitoring by a doctor, usually an endocrinologist or urologist.
Never take hormones without a prescription.

sources.label: Successful treatment of POIS with hCG (PMC)

entries.title: Biologics (omalizumab)
entries.summary: Omalizumab is an injected medicine that blocks IgE, an antibody involved in allergies. It is normally used for severe asthma and chronic hives.
reported: A 2024 case report described a substantial reduction in symptoms after several months, together with an antidepressant.
sideEffects: Reactions where the injection is given
Rarely, serious allergic reactions, so early doses are given under observation
cautions: Prescribed and monitored by a specialist only.

sources.label: POIS benefiting from omalizumab and antidepressant (J Med Case Reports, 2024)

entries.title: SSRIs and other psychiatric medicines
entries.summary: Some doctors have prescribed antidepressants (SSRIs) or, short term, benzodiazepines. These may help with mood and anxiety symptoms, and SSRIs can also delay ejaculation.
reported: Results in case reports are mixed.
sideEffects: SSRIs: nausea, sleep changes and sexual side effects; stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms
Benzodiazepines: drowsiness and a risk of dependence
cautions: Prescription only. Don't stop these suddenly without medical advice.
Benzodiazepines are generally only for short-term use.

sources.label: Post orgasmic illness syndrome: what do we know till now? (review, PMC)

entries.title: Supplements, diet and lifestyle
entries.summary: Patient communities share many strategies, from supplements to diet changes, exercise and massage. They haven't been studied for POIS, and accounts often contradict each other.
reported: Forum members report both success and no effect with the same approaches.
sideEffects: Supplements can interact with prescribed medicines
Niacin commonly causes flushing, and high doses can harm the liver
cautions: "Natural" doesn't mean safe: tell your doctor or pharmacist about any supplements you take.

redFlags: Seek medical care promptly for fever above 38.5 °C, trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, face or throat, chest pain or fainting. These are not typical POIS features.
